newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FOCUS-S&P affirms "one country two systems" with ratings.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S&P affirms "one country two systems" with ratings.

text.p: Standard and Poor's Corp raised the credit ratings of Hong Kong and China on Wednesday in a move seen as reflecting the two entities' strong fundamentals and the rating agency's confidence in "one country, two systems".
"What S&P is saying by continuing to rate Hong Kong and China differently is that Hong Kong's autonomy is rock solid," said Stephen Taran, research director at Lehman Brothers.
S&P raised China's sovereign rating to BBB-plus from BBB, citing the country's progress in economic reforms, its strong economy and its considerable external financial flexibility.
Hong Kong's long-term foreign currency rating was raised to A-plus from single-A, while its long-term local currency rating was upgraded to AA-minus from A-plus.
"The rating sends a signal to the market regarding the credibility of one country, two systems," said another analyst in Hong Kong.
Hong Kong's upgrade was based on the improvement in China's ratings, S&P said.

Unlike rival rating agency Moody's Investors Service, which rates Hong Kong and China equally at A3, S&P has long maintained that Hong Kong and China will remain separate enough after the transfer of sovereignty to merit separate ratings.
"As long as there is a significant difference between Hong Kong and China, we would expect there to be a gap in ratings," said Paul Coughlin, managing director at S&P in Hong Kong.
S&P said on Wednesday that the key factors underpinning the three-notch rating differential with China remain firmly in place as the transfer of sovereignty nears.
"China's incentives to respect Hong Kong's autonomy will continue to be strong, especially as economic reforms in the mainland deepen," S&P said in a statement.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
Coughlin said the handover process has been "remarkably smooth" and that S&P remains convinced the institutions put in place to assure Hong Kong's autonomy are solid.

The rollback in some civil liberties in conjunction with the transfer in power has been factored into the ratings for some years and does not indicate any change in China's stance toward the territory, S&P said.
"The changes that have been foreshadowed are not on the scale that would undermine Hong Kong's social stability and undermine Hong Kong's ability to repay debt," said Coughlin.
Coughlin acknowledged that Hong Kong's fiscal position is much stronger than is implied by an A-plus rating.

But he said the rating is constrained by the risk of misgovernance by Beijing over time as well as by Hong Kong's increasing economic and political integration with China, which leaves it vulnerable to any deterioration in the mainland's credit quality.
S&P also raised to BBB-plus from BBB the foreign currency rating of the State Development Bank of China.
Traders said the upgrade should give a boost to SDB's debt traded in the secondary market, which has been trading at a discount to the sovereign benchmark.

Other banks that had been rated equally with the sovereign -- Bank of China, Bank of Communications, China International Trust and Investment Corp and Industrial and Commercial Bank of China -- will not be upgraded to BBB-plus because they are becoming more commercialized and can no longer be considered sovereign credits, S&P said.
The rating agency in March had affirmed the ratings of these banks at BBB and revised their outlooks to stable from positive.
Also on Wednesday, S&P raised the ratings of several Hong Kong firms in conjunction with its upgrade of Hong Kong.
